records.name: Kogi
records.current_summary:
Kogi lies within Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.

Trans-specific risk is documented nationally: mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people were reported as common, especially in northern states, and the 2024 beating-death of a prominent transgender creator in the capital — after an earlier stabbing she had said left her fearing for her life — evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people, with an investigation announced but no accountability recorded in the sources.

No state-specific sources for Kogi survived audit, so no local divergence is claimed in either direction; sources do not identify Kogi among the northern states applying Sharia criminal provisions, but the national penalties apply in full.

sources.claim: BBC News (9 Aug 2024): murder of the Nigerian transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama' (33) — beaten body found on a highway in the capital; police opened an investigation; she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life. Article also notes that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.

SaharaReporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's updated Nigeria travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation — same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment; some northern states under Sharia law can prescribe the death penalty; the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Nigeria' entry records the national framework that applies in full in Kogi: the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union liable to 14 years' imprisonment and makes registering, operating or participating in 'gay clubs, societies and organisations' or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship liable to 10 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years, while the twelve Shari'a-administering northern states (with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism) impose harsher penalties, placing non-Shari'a states such as Kogi under the federal 14-year maximum. In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise; the entry records no similar ruling for the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions. It also notes the Constitution has no specific protections for sexual orientation and that there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: Country Policy and Information Note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics – Nigeria, June 2025 (GOV.UK)
sources.claim: The UK government's June 2025 country-policy note records the framework a visitor to Abia stands under: same-sex sexual acts between men carry up to 14 years' imprisonment under secular law, and the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union punishable by 14 years' imprisonment while giving 10 years to anyone who 'administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization' of one or supports the registration, operation and sustenance of gay clubs, societies, organisations, processions or meetings. The note states that sharia penal codes apply to Muslims in the 12 northern states (death as the maximum penalty for men, with at least four sharia death sentences imposed since 2022 and none carried out) and documents tens of LGBT+ arrests per year plus police and Islamic-police harassment including beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. The note does not reach Abia as a sharia state, matching the record's statement that the northern sharia provisions do not reach this southern state while federal penalties and the national arrest climate apply in full.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria – Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Nigeria article is the national-framework source for Abia: the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act 2013, in force from January 2014, criminalises same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and also punishes registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations and public displays of same-sex amorous relationships, with a 2022 federal court ruling striking down sections of the Act as unconstitutional. It lists the 12 northern states operating sharia criminal law for Muslims (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara) — Abia is not among them, corroborating the record's claim that the sharia provisions do not reach this southern state while the federal 14-year framework and the national climate of arrests and community hostility apply.

freshness_all.fact: Current (19 Aug 2026): UK travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, 14-year terms under SSMPA 2014 and death-penalty exposure under northern sharia provisions.
Incident record stands: transgender creator found dead Aug 2024; no decisive reversal reported since; violence risk against visibly trans people remains documented.

records.current_summary:
Ekiti lies within Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.

Trans-specific risk is evidenced nationally: a regional-magazine report on queer life in the federal capital documents threats and police raids alongside informal community organising, and community grief after the August 2024 killing of a prominent transgender creator; the report confirms that visibility itself is the trigger for enforcement and attack, a condition that travels to every state including Ekiti.

No state-specific sources for Ekiti survived audit, so no local divergence is claimed; as a southwestern state the northern Sharia provisions reported by the sources do not reach it, while the federal penalties, routine raid practice and strong church influence in local public life make concealed existence the prevailing security strategy for trans and queer residents and visitors alike.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act documents Ekiti State enforcement on the ground: on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened 'You will get 14 years in prison!'; HRW reports she was beaten at least twice over the period and, unable to use Ekiti health services safely, travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment. The report also records a September 2014 arrest at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti — a gay man's third arrest, released after two days in detention by paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend — and a 2014 incident in which a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti. These are the state-specific beatings, arrests and bribe-payments that the record's summary previously had no Ekiti source to cite.

records.name: Enugu
records.current_summary:
Federal criminal law governs visitor exposure in Enugu: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act reaches those who arrange, attend or promote same-sex weddings or publicly promote LGBTQ+ organisations. Government travel guidance issued by a foreign ministry in August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, and notes that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice.

Reporting on queer life under those laws documents threats and police raids alongside informal community organising, and public grief after the August 2024 murder of a well-known transgender figure in the federal capital. The murder and the raids it followed were reported in the capital, not in Enugu; no Enugu-specific statute, enforcement or protection is documented in the sources examined, so the state is assessed on the nationwide framework: criminalisation on the books, arbitrary policing, and violence that is rarely prosecuted.

sources.claim: SaharaReporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's updated travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, some northern states apply Sharia provisions that can prescribe the death penalty, and the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents the SSMPA's impact in Enugu State: Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told HRW she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure, saying 'For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married.' An Enugu-based activist told HRW that 'the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community' and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, forcing many to travel to Lagos and other states. This supplies the Enugu-specific social-coercion and healthcare-access findings absent from the record's existing sources.
